Hi Eric (list),

There's a bug in that formula I'm afraid.  I had forgotten to take the
series expansion to the forth power (2j where j is 2 in this case).  The
correct formula should be

((1-exp(-(y/0.4582)^-1.195)) / (1-exp(-(0/0.4582)^-1.195)) ) *

( (1- 1.954*(y/w)^4) / (1-1.954*(0/w)^4) )

This has already been corrected in the manual for Distance 6.0, which
should see general release very soon.  In the meantime, I'll send you
the revised manual chapter in a separate email.  Apologies for the
confusion.

  - len

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am trying to find densities and abundances for porpoises using Distance=

5.0 using nine years of line transect data from seabird surveys in
Washington state.=20

The study area is divided into three regions.  Region 1 has five subareas=

and each subarea has two components (nearshore and offshore).  Region 2 h=
as
20 subareas and each subarea has two components (nearshore and offshore).=
=20
Region 3 has 5 subareas and each subarea is just one component (offshore)=
.=20
Every year of effort has two replications.=20

Ideally I would do one analysis for all the data pooled over time and spa=
ce,
and do individual analyses filtering out data for each year, region,
subunit, and component.=20=20

Currently, my Distance project is set up as follows:=20=20
Region labels are r1, r2, r3 for the three different regions, and region
areas are their areas in KM2.
Since the same lines are repeated twice a year for nine years, the line
labels are unique names including the year (2000 - 2008), replication (re=
p1
or rep2), region (r1, r2, r3), and subarea/component.  For example,
2000rep1r102N would stand for year 2000, replicate 1, region 1, subarea 0=
2
component Nearshore; 2007rep2r242O would stand for year 2007 replicate 2
region 2 subunit 42 component Offshore, etc., and the line lengths are
whatever they are in KM.
Observation level contains cluster size, perp. distance, and a host of ot=
her
parameters including "Year", "Component", "replicate".=20=20

My initial analysis looking at all data pooled over time and space ran we=
ll
with two warnings (parameters constrained to obtain monotonicity), howeve=
r
when I tried to filter the data for individual years using data filter
Observation [Year] =3D 2000, the results filtered out the samples from 20=
00
but used the effort for all years combined, not just 2000.  The same issu=
e
happens when I filter for Observation [Replicate] =3D "r1" or anything el=

Washington state.=20

and each subarea has two components (nearshore and offshore).  Region 2 h=
as
20 subareas and each subarea has two components (nearshore and offshore).=
=20
Region 3 has 5 subareas and each subarea is just one component (offshore)=
.=20
Every year of effort has two replications.=20

Ideally I would do one analysis for all the data pooled over time and spa=
ce,
and do individual analyses filtering out data for each year, region,
subunit, and component.=20=20

Currently, my Distance project is set up as follows:=20=20
Region labels are r1, r2, r3 for the three different regions, and region
areas are their areas in KM2.
Since the same lines are repeated twice a year for nine years, the line
labels are unique names including the year (2000 - 2008), replication (re=
p1
or rep2), region (r1, r2, r3), and subarea/component.  For example,
2000rep1r102N would stand for year 2000, replicate 1, region 1, subarea 0=
2
component Nearshore; 2007rep2r242O would stand for year 2007 replicate 2
region 2 subunit 42 component Offshore, etc., and the line lengths are
whatever they are in KM.
Observation level contains cluster size, perp. distance, and a host of ot=
her
parameters including "Year", "Component", "replicate".=20=20

My initial analysis looking at all data pooled over time and space ran we=
ll
with two warnings (parameters constrained to obtain monotonicity), howeve=
r
when I tried to filter the data for individual years using data filter
Observation [Year] =3D 2000, the results filtered out the samples from 20=
00
but used the effort for all years combined, not just 2000.  The same issu=
e
happens when I filter for Observation [Replicate] =3D "r1" or anything el=
se in
the Observation level.

Then I tried to filter using Sample level [Label] LIKE "2000%" in the hop=
es
that the SQL expression would use the lines that started with year 2000, =
but
I got an error stating "encountered a problem writing to the data file
C:blahblahblah"=20=20

So after all this, I have two questions:

1.  Most importantly, is my Distance project set up correctly to begin wi=
th?
2.  What is the best way to filter by year/replicate/component/region?

Hopefully all of the above makes sense.

Any help or advice would be extremely welcome at this point.=20=20

Thanks,
-Adam

messages.body_plain:
Tina, a few brief responses, but your questions are largely answered in=20
the 2001 book.
> > I am a Distance beginner, and am currently reading the manual and worki=
ng through examples to start my analysis of a survey I conducted in a Pan=
amanian National Park on 3 rare bird species.  I have some basic question=
s at this time, and also any general tips you have as well would be appre=
ciated.
> >
> > Some background:  The survey was in a national park consisting of one h=
uge island, a couple smaller islands and many islets.  I placed six 1 km =
transect lines on the main island (5 transects) and one small island (1 t=
ransect).  There are no "stratum" in this case, all transects were places=
 in forest, though quality of forest varied.  I did place transects on th=
e west, east and north of the big island, and at different elevations to =
cover as much territory as possible. =20
> >  =20
I'm not sure what your objective is, but if it is to estimate population=20
size in the islands, you need a randomised design, typically a set of=20
systematically-spaced parallel lines randomly positioned over the islands.
> > We have 7 surveys of each transect in the dry season, and 6 surveys in =
the rainy season. Only one year of data. =20
> >
> > One species was ubiquitous (at all 6 transects) and abundant (up to 20-=
30 birds PER transect).  One species was ubiquitous but not abundant, onl=
y 1 pair to 4 pair per transect; sample size is low.  The third species w=
as only found at ONE transect (the highest elevation site) and only adult=
 males were seen regularly (a few juvenile males OR females were seen, bu=
t they cannot be distinguished from each other for certain).   =20
> >
> > First question:  how do I deal with replicate transects? As mentioned: =
I have 7 visits to the same transects in the dry season, and 6 visits to =
those transects in the rainy season.
> >  =20
Within a season, pool detections and define your effort to be line=20
length multiplied by the number of times you covered the line.
> > Second question:  How do I set up the data for separate rainy and dry s=
eason analyses? =20
> >  =20
It could be separate projects, or you could define a field corresponding=20
to season, and e.g. poststratify by season.
> > Third question:  Is there a model best used for small sample size?  In =
the book, the recommended sample size was at least 40, but is that total =
over all transects, all visits, or what?  As stated above: for one specie=
s I have one to 4 pairs of birds per transect (6 transects total).
> >  =20
At least 40 for each det fn you model. So within a season in your case -=20
or if you can assume the same det fn by season, it would be your total=20
sample size. You can also use the mcds engine in Distance, and enter=20
season as a factor, so you can still pool data across seasons but=20
without having to assume the det fn does not vary by season. You can=20
also consider pooling across species, with species as a factor. See

Marques, T.A., Thomas, L., Fancy, S.G. and Buckland, S.T. 2007.=20
Improving estimates of bird density using multiple covariate distance=20
sampling. /The Auk/ *124*, 1229-1243.

Alldredge, M. W., K. H. Pollock, T. R. Simons and S. A. Shriner. 2007.=20
Multiple-species analysis of point count data: A more parsimonious=20
modelling framework. Journal of Applied Ecology 44:281=96290.

> > Fourth question: Can I/Should I use this type of analyses for the third=
 species, which was absent at 5 transects and present only at 1 transect?=
  Would an estimate of population over the entire study area be feasible/=
desirable with such a situation?  If so, is there anything to take into c=
onsideration for analyses?
> >  =20
If you record a species from just one subjectively placed transect, then=20
there is no basis for estimating popn size throughout the islands.
> > Fifth question:  I assume that sex should be entered where we have this=
 data, as that will affect the population estimate?  As mentioned above, =
the third species that was only at one transect was almost entirely adult=
 males, with only a few birds that could have been juvy males or females.=
 =20
> >  =20
If males are much more detectable than females, I would recommend=20
analysing males only, and hope that gives a good estimate of number of=20
territories. If they have similar detectabilities, you can either pool=20
or get separate estimates for males and females. The latter gives you a=20
check of whether methods are working OK, if you expect similar numbers=20
of both.

Steve Buckland
> > That's all for now, more to come I am sure. =20
> >
> > Thanks to all in advance for your valuable help,
> > Tina Blewett

find that observers are no better at putting detections into 5 or 6
distance intervals than in estimating actual distances.  Not sure how
many observers you will have, but laser rangefinders are quite
inexpensive, so it may be worth investing in some.

messages.subject_clean: Distance sampling using predefined bin size
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the clarification. Your original message didn't say anything
about a breeding bird survey but not being a bird biologist that would
probably have been lost on me anyhow.  But also, given that this list is
read by many different folks it is important to be clear.  I didn't want
anyone to interpret this to mean that they didn't need to record group
size unless most are singles and just a few pairs are encountered.  I
have seen examples where people have done as you said and the group size
varied substantially and the information was lost.

If the sightings are only single birds then you are fine but if you have
a mix of singles and pairs, then these should be recorded separately or
your variance estimate for detection is not valid because the code will
treat a group of 2 birds as 2 separate sightings of single birds.  This
will tend to underestimate the variance and the impact will depend on
how many pairs you see relative to singles and the relative importance
of the detection variance relative to the encounter variance.  If you
have a sufficient number of lines/points (per stratum) you could use a
bootstrap to obtain a better variance estimate.

regards--jeff
